question: Two years after penetrating keratoplasty, a patient presents with a sudden decrease in vision, ciliary congestion, and a horizontal line of keratic precipitates progressing across the graft from the periphery to the centre (Khodadoust line). Which type of graft rejection is this?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epithelial rejection presents as an irregular line of elevated epithelium (epithelial rejection line) traversing the graft surface — no KPs on the endothelium. It is the mildest and most reversible form.

Subepithelial (Krachmer's spots) rejection shows nummular (coin-shaped) subepithelial infiltrates, similar to those in adenoviral keratitis. No endothelial KP line. This is not the Khodadoust line pattern.

Correct. The Khodadoust line = a line of keratic precipitates on the endothelium sweeping across the graft — pathognomonic of endothelial rejection. This is the MOST serious type; if untreated it causes irreversible endothelial failure. Treat immediately with intensive topical steroids.
Stromal rejection causes diffuse stromal oedema and vascularisation without a discrete endothelial KP line. The Khodadoust line specifically indicates endothelial immune attack.

overallFeedback.feedback: Khodadoust line = line of KPs on the endothelium = ENDOTHELIAL rejection. This is the most dangerous type. Compare: epithelial line (surface), Krachmer's spots (subepithelial nummular), stromal oedema (stromal).
Correct! Khodadoust line = endothelial rejection — the most severe type. Treat immediately with prednisolone acetate 1% every hour + systemic steroids. Delay = irreversible graft failure.
